extracted.intended_audience: beginners and people interested in learning improv for performance, personal growth, or professional development (e.g., prospective Change Through Play students)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical beginner's guide to improvisation covering core principles, differences between short- and long-form, warm-ups, and ways to get started for both performers and non-performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Yes, And” Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the foundation of all improvisation. Accept what your scene partner says (that’s the “yes”) and build on it (that’s the “and”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If your partner says, 'We’re on a spaceship,' you should not contradict with 'No, we’re actually in a Starbucks.' Instead say, 'Yes, and we’re almost out of fuel!' Use this to keep scenes moving and collaboratively create new offers rather than blocking them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay in the Moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t try to plan ahead. Improv works best when you focus on reacting to what’s happening right now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pre-planning jokes or scene beats; respond to current offers and discoveries in the scene. Presence enables authentic reactions and emergent storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening is Key
rubrics_metrics.description: Great improv scenes happen when performers listen carefully to each other. It’s not about who can be the funniest—it’s about responding authentically to your scene partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice active listening so you hear and use your partner’s offers. Prioritize building on what’s given rather than competing for laughs or attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Warm-Up Exercises (e.g., Zip, Zap, Zop)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warm-ups get your mind and reflexes engaged before playing. Zip, Zap, Zop: one person says 'zip' while pointing to another, who says 'zap' and points to someone else, who says 'zop.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the rhythm moving quickly without losing focus. Regular warm-ups sharpen focus, timing, and ensemble responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short Form vs Long Form (choose format to fit goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short form is fast-paced, punchy, and game-driven (often aiming for quick laughs). Long form is more like an unscripted play, allowing development of characters, relationships, and narratives over multiple interconnected scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want quick games and immediate laughs, short form fits; for deeper storytelling and collaborative narrative-building, focus on long form structures like the Harold. Align format with learning goals (e.g., wit/sharpness vs. storytelling/depth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Audience Suggestions as Seeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers use audience suggestions to create scenes and launch improvisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat suggestions as a springboard — accept them and build. Historically a hallmark of modern improv (e.g., Dudley Riggs); learn to harvest specific elements from a suggestion rather than dismissing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long Form: Develop Characters, Relationships, and Narrative (e.g., The Harold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long form allows performers space to develop characters, relationships, and narratives over time. The Harold begins with an audience suggestion and blossoms into a series of scenes woven into a cohesive, narrative-driven piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on sustaining character choices, tracking callbacks, and weaving scenes together. Emphasize real, human moments rather than only gag-based humor to build depth across multiple scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv for Personal Growth and Professional Skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv helps build confidence, adaptability, creativity, and is often used in business training to improve communication, collaboration, and leadership skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame exercises toward desired outcomes (e.g., public speaking, team communication). Expect benefits like improved presence, adaptability, and teamwork that transfer outside performance contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anyone Can Learn Improv (accessibility and supportive entry paths)
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t need to be the next John Belushi to get started. Improv is accessible to introverts and extroverts alike and can be learned through practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a supportive class or jams; progression can include taking classes, joining jams, starting a group, or hosting jams. Emphasize a nonjudgmental, growth-focused environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Improv Styles — pick what interests you
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv comes in many flavors: improv comedy, musical improv, improvisational theatre (story-driven), game-show/competitive improv, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose styles that match your goals (e.g., musical skills for musical improv, narrative sensibility for long form). Understand distinctions from related forms: sketch is scripted, stand-up is typically pre-written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize Collaboration Over Individual Punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective improv is collaborative; it's not about who can be the funniest but about creating something together and responding authentically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-upmanship and punchline-only contributions. Support partners’ offers, make strong choices that serve the scene, and look for moments to elevate ensemble truth rather than individual jokes.
